Thanks for the profile, Maya — this is helpful. Quick technical readout and recommendation for the SOW:

Summary recommendations:
- Reserved slab: provision 12 Tesla-V100-equivalent GPUs (or equivalent TFLOP-matched instances) to cover baseline and P95 target for real-time traffic. This assumes average request complexity in CSV; we can refine with a small eval run.
- Elastic headroom: 6 preemptible GPUs in a transient slab (ephemeral pool) that can be used for burst traffic. These are lower-cost, preemptible instances with <2 minute reclamation notice.
- Eviction policy: real-time workload pinned to reserved slab (no eviction); background batch jobs are lowest priority and will be preempted first. For long spikes (>30 minutes) we recommend automated fallback to a cheaper model variant for some requests to preserve throughput.
- Autoscale thresholds:
  * Prewarm trigger: sustained 120% of baseline for 90s -> spin up 1 ephemeral node
  * Aggressive scale: sustained 300% baseline -> scale ephemeral pool in 30s increments up to configured cap
  * Cooldown: 5 minutes of sub-110% baseline before scale-down
- Billing: support monthly credit pool (we can pre-allocate X GPU-hours as credits) + pay-as-you-go true-up. Sales ops (Laura) can map credit-to-cost in the SOW.

Operational notes:
- We can instrument a telemetry hook to mark requests as "real-time" vs "batch" so routing honors the reserved slab.
- For launch-day 12x spikes, recommend a temporary manual uplift window (ops-assisted) rather than full auto-scale to reduce risk.

Next steps I propose:
1) Small 24-hour benchmark using HelixAI sample to validate GPU-per-req numbers (I can spin this up with engineering).
2) Laura to draft SOW language for reserved slab + ephemeral headroom + credit model.
3) Procurement to confirm preferred credit size and billing cadence.
